## 5 Baron’s Rebuttal of Borch
Baron rebuts Borch’s paradox in two steps. First comes the proposition that decision-making based on just the two parameters, mean and variance, implies an underlying quadratic utility function.
Specifically, for risk-averse quadratic utility u(x)=2ax-x^2, the expected utility is E[u(x)]=2aμ-(μ^2+σ^2).

Johnstone and Lindley (2011) have more recently given an elementary proof revealing that, in the absence of any further premise, MV necessitates quadratic utility.

[PyPortfolioOpt](https://pyportfolioopt.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html)

Mathematical optimization is a very difficult problem in general, particularly when we are dealing with complex objectives and constraints. However, **convex optimization** problems are a well-understood class of problems, which happen to be incredibly useful for finance. A convex problem has the following form:

$$
\begin{matrix} & \underset{\mathbf{x}}{\text{minimise}} & & f \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right) \\ & \text{subject to} & & g_{i} \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right) \leq 0 , i = 1 , \ldots , m \\ & & & A \mathbf{x} = b ,\end{matrix}
$$

where $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, and $f \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right) , g_{i} \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right)$ are convex functions. [[1]](https://pyportfolioopt.readthedocs.io/en/latest/MeanVariance.html#id2)

Fortunately, portfolio optimization problems (with standard objectives and constraints) are convex. This allows us to immediately apply the vast body of theory as well as the refined solving routines – accordingly, the main difficulty is inputting our specific problem into a solver.

PyPortfolioOpt aims to do the hard work for you, allowing for one-liners like `ef.min_volatility()` to generate a portfolio that minimises the volatility, while at the same time allowing for more complex problems to be built up from modular units. This is all possible thanks to [cvxpy](https://www.cvxpy.org/), the _fantastic_ python-embedded modelling language for convex optimization upon which PyPortfolioOpt’s efficient frontier functionality lies.

Mean–Variance Optimization (MVO) is a central framework for portfolio construction: choose weights that balance expected return against risk as measured by variance.

In its classical form, MVO is elegant, convex (under mild conditions), and analytically tractable. keenable.snippet:
This study develops a multi-period portfolio method for investors who face no-shorting constraints and wish to use entropy regularization without losing the tractable structure of the original mean–variance problem. A standard fixed temperature can preserve convexity but generally destroys the simple Bellman recursion under no-shorting. The proposed state-dependent temperature retains the piecewise-linear feedback form and provides a clear condition for when the backward recursion remains convex.

Portfolio constraints substantially alter this structure. Under no-shorting, risky positions are restricted to the nonnegative orthant, so the unconstrained linear feedback rule and quadratic recursion no longer apply directly.

The positive-mean condition is the standard positive-risk-premium assumption used in the no-shorting formulation of Cui et al. (2014).

This paper studies entropy regularization in the discrete-time mean–variance problem under no-shorting. A standard fixed absolute temperature can preserve convexity but generally destroys the homogeneous Bellman structure that makes the constrained problem tractable. We show that matching the entropy scale to the quadratic wealth-gap structure restores the piecewise-quadratic value function and the finite-dimensional backward recursion. The resulting continuation coefficients, however, must remain positive to preserve recursive convexity.

keenable.snippet: In the second part of this work, we examine the premise of Levy and Markowitz (1979) that "the MVC deduces the maximization of the expected utility of an investor, under any approximately quadratic utility function, without making any further assumption on the distribution of the lotteries". keenable.title: Expected Utility Regret Rule: Minimax and Bayes Optimal Portfolio Choice
keenable.snippet: This study considers the problem of portfolio choice, where we recommend a portfolio to an investor to maximize the expected utility of their wealth. Our goal is to construct an asymptotically optimal portfolio choice rule in terms of expected utility regret, the difference between the expected utility of an oracle investor and that achieved by a portfolio chosen from data. We propose the Expected Utility Regret (EUR) rule, which jointly selects a portfolio class and estimates its weights. In a regular parametric return model, a single EUR rule attains both the minimax and the Bayes lower bounds, including their leading constants, without using the evaluation prior. We then derive the mean–variance and risk-parity portfolios as special cases of this framework. First, under smooth increasing and concave utility, the EUR rule and the sample mean–variance portfolio attain the same leading expected regret when expected excess returns approach zero sufficiently fast. Second, when the returns divided by their volatilities have a joint distribution that does not depend on the order of the assets, the EUR rule and the risk-parity portfolio coincide.

keenable-realtime.snippet: This study considers the problem of portfolio choice, where we recommend a portfolio to an investor to maximize the expected utility of their wealth. Our goal is to construct an asymptotically optimal portfolio choice rule in terms of expected utility regret, the difference between the expected utility of an oracle investor and that achieved by a portfolio chosen from data. ## What Is Quadratic Utility  
Two concepts you need to understand very well before we continue:  
- **Risk aversion**: How comfortable a person is with the risk of uncertain outcomes in exchange for a given return.
- **Utility functions**: Measures the satisfaction (happiness) you get from different bundles of goods, services, or investments. Utility functions are a way to measure risk aversion.  
The purpose of these concepts? They help you *quantify* the demand for assets, therefore better estimating their price. This is essential for asset pricing and valuing [future uncertain cash flows](https://financestu.com/introduction-asset-pricing/).  
**The quadratic utility function says an investor values different investment opportunities under uncertainty based on their mean wealth and the variance of their wealth.**  
This is what’s called **mean-variance preferences**—for any probability distribution of wealth, the expected utility depends *only* on the mean and variance of wealth, regardless of the probability distribution of the outcomes.  
It is called *quadratic* because it is a quadratic function of the individual’s wealth or income (or unit of consumption, or anything you’d rather have more of).  
A [quadratic function](https://www.cuemath.com/calculus/quadratic-functions/) is a polynomial function in which the highest exponent of a variable is two.

The mean-variance utility postulates that random variables with the same mean and variance should be equally desirable. This paper presents and discusses necessary and sufficient preference-based axioms for the existence of mean-variance utility in which any condition on variances but mean-values is not explicitly specified. Expected utility (EU) maximization and mean-variance (MV) analysis are two tenets in rational decision making under risk. parallel-turbo.title: Mean–variance approximations to expected utility
parallel-turbo.snippet: It is often asserted that the application of mean–variance analysis assumes normal (Gaussian) return distributions or quadratic utility functions. This common mistake confuses sufficient versus necessary conditions for the applicability of modern portfolio theory. If one believes (as does the author) that choice should be guided by the expected utility maxim, then the necessary and sufficient condition for the practical use of mean–variance analysis is that a careful choice from a mean–variance efficient frontier will approximately maximize expected utility for a wide variety of concave (risk-averse) utility functions. This paper reviews a half-century of research on mean–variance approximations to expected utility.

parallel-turbo.snippet:
* • We show that the three quadratic optimization problems are mathematically equivalent but not from a stochastic point of view.
* • We derive the probabilities that the estimated solutions of the Markowitz problem and the quadratic utility problem are mean–variance efficient.

Abstract

In the paper, we consider three quadratic optimization problems which are frequently applied in portfolio theory, i.e., the Markowitz mean–variance problem as well as the problems based on the mean–variance utility function and the quadratic utility. Conditions are derived under which the solutions of these three optimization procedures coincide and are lying on the efficient frontier, the set of mean–variance optimal portfolios. It is shown that the solutions of the Markowitz optimization problem and the quadratic utility problem are not always mean–variance efficient.
The conditions for the mean–variance efficiency of the solutions depend on the unknown parameters of the asset returns.

Every theoretical model in science is a deliberate simplification of reality. Understanding why these conclusions follow from the assumptions, and what happens when each assumption is relaxed, is essential for understanding both the power and the limitations of the model. ## Quadratic Utility Functions

## 1. Quadratic Utility in Plain English

A **utility function** turns an amount of wealth into a score of how satisfied an investor is with it. Economists since Bernoulli (1738) have drawn that score as a curve that rises but bends over: the first extra million matters more than the tenth. An investor who scores outcomes on such a bent curve dislikes risk, because a 50/50 gamble between more and less wealth scores lower than its average outcome for sure. The general idea, and how a portfolio is chosen by maximising the average score, is set out in Utility Maximization in Portfolio Construction. This post is about the simplest such curve.

*U(W) = W − (b/2) W2*

Here *W* is wealth at the end of the period (we measure it in units where 1 = USD 1 million) and *b* is a positive number that sets how fast satisfaction tapers off. The slope of the curve, which economists call **marginal utility**, is U′(W) = 1 − bW: it falls in a straight line as wealth grows and hits zero at W = 1/b.

Picture walking up a smooth hill. Each step forward raises you a little less than the last, and at the summit, W = 1/b, the climb stops. Walk further and you start going *down*. That summit is the **bliss point**. Below it, quadratic utility behaves like a sensible risk-averse investor. Above it, the formula says more money makes the investor less happy, which no real investor believes. Keep that hill in mind: the whole story of quadratic utility is that it gives mean-variance analysis an exact foundation, and pays for it with two defects that both come from the hill having a top.

**The Arrow–Pratt measures of risk aversion** are two local indices of the curvature of a von Neumann–Morgenstern utility function that quantify how strongly a decision maker dislikes uncertainty in wealth. They were developed independently by John W. Pratt in the 1964 *Econometrica* paper "Risk Aversion in the Small and in the Large" and by Kenneth J. Arrow in his 1965 Yrjö Jahnsson lectures on the theory of risk-bearing. The **coefficient of absolute risk aversion**, *A*(*w*) = −*u*″(*w*) / *u*′(*w*), and the **coefficient of relative risk aversion**, *R*(*w*) = *w A*(*w*), allow economists to compare risk attitudes across individuals and wealth levels, and to derive testable predictions in finance, insurance, and macroeconomics.

## Concavity and the Need for a Measure

Under expected utility theory, an agent with utility function *u* over wealth *w* is risk averse if and only if *u* is concave, so that the agent prefers receiving the expected value of a gamble for certain to facing the gamble itself. Concavity, equivalent to *u*″ < 0 for twice-differentiable functions, delivers a qualitative classification but not a quantitative one. The second derivative alone is not a satisfactory measure, because expected utility representations are unique only up to positive affine transformations *a* + *b u* with *b* > 0, and *u*″ changes with the scale *b*. A meaningful index must be invariant to such transformations.

The ratio −*u*″ / *u*′ satisfies this requirement, since both numerator and denominator scale by *b*. It is also the natural quantity: it measures the rate at which marginal utility falls in proportion to its level, and it connects to the willingness to pay for insurance, as the next section shows. Related to marginal utility, the measure captures how quickly the value of an additional unit of wealth declines.

## Quadratic Programming in Portfolio Construction

## 1. What Quadratic Programming Means, in Plain English

A **quadratic program**, or QP, is an optimisation problem with two features. The thing you are minimising or maximising (the **objective**) contains squared terms and products of pairs of unknowns, such as x2 or x×y. And every rule the answer must obey (each **constraint**) is linear: a sum that must equal something, or a quantity that must stay above or below a limit. Nothing more exotic than that.

Here is the picture to keep in mind. Imagine a marble in a smooth bowl. Left alone, it rolls to the lowest point, and you can find that point with one formula. Now put fences inside the bowl. If the lowest point lies inside the fenced area, the marble still ends up there and the fences do nothing. If it lies outside, the marble rolls until it rests against one or more fences and stops at the lowest point it can reach. Solving a QP is mostly about one question: *which fences does the marble lean on?*

The fences also tell you something valuable. How hard the marble presses on a fence measures how much better you could do if that fence moved a little. That pressure is the fence’s **shadow price**, and it is the most useful by-product of a QP for a portfolio manager.

Why does this matter for investing? Because the workhorse problems of portfolio construction – mean-variance optimisation, minimum-variance portfolios, minimising tracking error against a benchmark – are all QPs. ## Utility Maximization in Portfolio Construction

Mean-variance optimisation asks you for one number, a risk-aversion coefficient, and hands back a portfolio. Utility maximisation asks a bigger question first: how much is a whole range of possible outcomes worth to this particular investor? This post sets up that question for beginners, solves it for three classic utility functions on the same four illustrative asset classes, and measures when the answer differs from plain mean-variance and when it does not. Every number below was computed, and the data are illustrative, not market data.

## 1. Utility Maximization in Plain English

A portfolio is a bet on a whole spread of possible futures, not on one number. The expected return tells you the middle of that spread and the volatility tells you its width, but an investor lives through only one outcome. **Utility maximisation** is the rule that turns the whole spread into a single score. Daniel Bernoulli (1738) proposed it to explain why nobody pays a fortune to play a coin game whose average payout is infinite; von Neumann and Morgenstern (1944) later showed that anyone whose choices obey a few consistency rules behaves as if maximising expected utility.

The recipe has three steps. First, list every possible end-of-year wealth and its probability. Second, pass each wealth through a **utility function** U(W): a curve that rises with wealth W but flattens as you get richer, so an extra dollar matters less to a rich investor than to a poor one. Third, average the utilities, weighting by probability. The portfolio with the highest average wins.

A coin example makes it concrete. Start with wealth 1.

Most portfolio advice talks in percentages: put 60% in equities, hold 40% in bonds. Exponential utility talks in dollars. It describes an investor who decides how many dollars to put at risk, and then keeps that dollar amount the same whether she is managing USD 1 million or USD 10 million. That sounds odd for a person, but it is exactly how many trading desks, market makers and risk budgets behave, and it comes with a mathematical gift: under normal returns it turns into ordinary mean-variance optimisation with no approximation at all. ## Markowitz Efficient Frontier Explained

The efficient frontier is one of the most powerful and enduring constructs in quantitative finance. Introduced by Harry Markowitz in his 1952 paper \"Portfolio Selection\" published in the Journal of Finance, it represents the geometric locus of optimal portfolios in mean-variance space, portfolios that offer the highest possible expected return for any given level of portfolio variance, or equivalently, the lowest possible variance for any given level of expected return. The efficient frontier did not merely refine existing investment practice. It revolutionised it, replacing the informal and qualitative approach to portfolio construction that had dominated investment management with a mathematically precise optimisation framework grounded in probability theory, linear algebra, and constrained quadratic programming. In doing so, it provided the conceptual and computational foundation for the Capital Asset Pricing Model, the Arbitrage Pricing Theory, the Black-Litterman model, and virtually every quantitative approach to portfolio management that followed. To understand the efficient frontier deeply is to understand the mathematical spine of modern investment theory. This post develops the efficient frontier from its statistical foundations through its analytical derivation, examining its geometric properties, its sensitivity to inputs, its extensions to include a risk-free asset, and its practical limitations in real-world portfolio construction.

Published: 28 Jan 2022, Last Modified: 13 Feb 2023ICLR 2022 SubmittedReaders: Everyone. **Keywords:** Reinforcement learning, Mean-variance tradeoff. **Abstract:** Risk management is critical in decision making, and mean-variance (MV) trade-off is one of the most common criteria. However, in reinforcement learning (RL) for sequential decision making under uncertainty, most of the existing methods for MV control suffer from computational difficulties owing to calculating the gradient of the variance term. In this paper, in contrast to strict MV control, we consider learning MV efficient policies that achieve Pareto efficiency regarding MV trade-off. The EQUMRL does not suffer from the computational difficulties because it does not include gradient estimation of the variance. We confirm that the maximizer of the objective in the EQUMRL directly corresponds to an MV efficient policy under a certain condition. We conduct experiments with benchmark settings to demonstrate the effectiveness of the EQUMRL. **One-sentence Summary:** Learning a policy achieving a Pareto efficiency in the sense of the mean variance trade-off by maximizing the expected quadratic utility function. ultimate.snippet: This study considers the problem of portfolio choice, where we recommend a portfolio to an investor to maximize the expected utility of their wealth. Our goal is to construct an asymptotically optimal portfolio choice rule in terms of expected utility regret, the difference between the expected utility of an oracle investor and that achieved by a portfolio chosen from data. We propose the Expected Utility Regret (EUR) rule, which jointly selects a portfolio class and estimates its weights. In a regular parametric return model, a single EUR rule attains both the minimax and the Bayes lower bounds, including their leading constants, without using the evaluation prior. We then derive the mean–variance and risk-parity portfolios as special cases of this framework. First, under smooth increasing and concave utility, the EUR rule and the sample mean–variance portfolio attain the same leading expected regret when expected excess returns approach zero sufficiently fast. Second, when the returns divided by their volatilities have a joint distribution that does not depend on the order of the assets, the EUR rule and the risk-parity portfolio coincide.
